pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 7–9; understand that tropical rainforests have a hot (25–30°C) and very wet (>2000 mm rain/year) climate ALL YEAR, and that this constant heat + moisture drives rapid plant growth and extraordinary biodiversity.
• Standards — UK: DfE KS2 Geography (climate zones, biomes; compare a contrasting region with the UK) and Science 'Living things and their habitats' (conditions suiting organisms).
• Standards — US: NGSS 3-ESS2-2 (climate of a region) and K-2/3-5 weather-vs-climate; MS-ESS2-6 (uneven heating/latitude drives climate) as a stretch.
• Operational details — fix the two variables and their CONSEQUENCE: consistently hot AND consistently wet → ideal growing conditions year-round (no cold season to stop growth, no dry season to halt it). Contrast explicitly with the child's own climate (UK ~ cooler, far less rain, strong seasons) using real numbers, and with a desert (hot but DRY → little life) to show it's the COMBINATION that matters. Distinguish weather (today) from climate (the usual pattern over years). Numbers as anchors: 25–30°C, >2000 mm.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (7): state that rainforests are hot and wet all year. Tier B (8): give the rough figures (25–30°C, >2000 mm) and say why that suits fast plant growth. Tier C (9): compare to the UK/local climate with numbers and explain why hot-AND-wet (not just hot) produces such biodiversity.
bestPractices: Teach the two variables together with their consequence: hot AND wet → ideal year-round growth.
Contrast with the child's own climate using real numbers, and with a hot DESERT to prove the combination (not heat alone) matters.
Distinguish weather (today) from climate (the usual multi-year pattern) explicitly.
Use the numeric anchors 25–30°C and >2000 mm so 'hot and wet' is quantified, not vague.
Link 'no seasons to stop growth' to the lushness and biodiversity the child has already met.
keyRepresentations: A climate graph (temperature line + rainfall bars) flat and high across all 12 months.
A three-way compare: rainforest vs UK vs desert (temperature, rainfall, amount of life).
Two dials — temperature and rainfall — as the causal variables.
A greening/withering plot that responds to the climate conditions.
commonMisconceptions: 'Rainforests have a hot season and a cold season like us' — they are hot and wet consistently, with little seasonal change.
'Hot places are all like deserts' — deserts are hot but DRY; it's the added water that makes rainforest life.
'Weather and climate are the same' — weather is today; climate is the long-term usual pattern.
'It only rains sometimes' — rainforests receive very high rainfall spread through the year.
'Any warmth makes a rainforest' — without high rainfall you get grassland or desert, not rainforest.

learn.summary: For ages 7–9: understand that tropical rainforests are consistently hot (about 25–30°C) and very wet (over 2000 mm rain/year) all year, with little seasonal change, and that it is the COMBINATION of constant heat AND constant moisture — not heat alone — that drives rapid plant growth and extraordinary biodiversity. Learners quantify 'hot and wet' with real numbers, compare the rainforest with their own climate and with a hot desert, and distinguish weather (today) from climate (the usual multi-year pattern).

activities.title: Two dials: heat and water together
feedback: If a learner credits heat alone: reset rainfall low while keeping heat high and ask what grows — the hot-but-dry desert shows heat is not enough.
If a learner credits water alone: lower the temperature while keeping rain high and show the cool, wet scene, where growth is slower and there are fewer kinds of plants and animals.
If both are high and growth maxes out: prompt them to state the combination rule, not just name the result.
Confirm success when the learner can predict each of the three outcomes before changing the settings and explain WHY the combination matters.
activities.rationale: Climate→growth is a two-variable cause-effect relationship; letting learners vary temperature and rainfall independently (via sliders, dials, or a teacher-controlled paper/card version) lets them test that the combination matters rather than being told it. Live feedback — a greening/withering plot and a growth meter — makes the consequence visible as each variable changes. These interactive elements are optional examples of how to make the mechanism concrete, not required mechanisms, and their comparative effectiveness is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: Tropical rainforests are consistently hot (about 25–30°C) and receive over 2000 mm of rain per year, with little seasonal variation, producing ideal year-round growing conditions
learnerActions: Start with a bare patch of ground shown on screen or on paper, controlled by two settings: TEMPERATURE and RAINFALL.
Set temperature high but rainfall low, and describe/predict what the patch becomes (hot but dry → cracked desert, little life such as a lone cactus).

Set rainfall high but temperature low, and describe the result (cool and wet → slower growth and fewer kinds of plants and animals, e.g. mosses and ferns on a cold, wet hillside; real cool, wet places can still be green, but they have much less variety of life than a tropical rainforest).
Set BOTH high to tropical values (about 28°C, soaking wet, all year) and describe the result (towering trees, vines, many animals, a 'growth/biodiversity' meter near maximum).
Jump between preset settings for 'Rainforest/Amazon', 'UK' (cool, moderate rain, modest life) and 'Desert' (hot, dry) and compare the amount of life in each.
State in your own words the rule you discover: it is heat AND water held high together, all year with no off-season, that produces the most crowded, fastest-growing habitat.
activities.intendedInsight: Rainforest lushness comes from constant heat AND constant heavy rain combined; either variable alone (hot desert, or cool wet hillside) gives a very different, much less biodiverse place.

activities.title: Three-way climate compare with real numbers
feedback: If a learner says the rainforest and desert are 'both just hot places': point to the rainfall column — heat + heavy rain = rainforest, heat + little rain = desert.
If a learner omits numbers: prompt for the anchors (25–30°C, >2000 mm) and the local comparison.
Confirm success when the learner uses figures to contrast all three places and names rainfall as the key rainforest-vs-desert difference.
activities.rationale: Comparing a contrasting region with the UK using real temperature and rainfall figures is a stated curriculum aim and anchors the abstract 'hot and wet' in quantities. A comparison display (bar charts, representative organisms) delivers the facts cleanly; building or annotating a comparison requires the learner to produce and organise the figures rather than only recognise them.
sourceClaims: KS2 geography requires describing and comparing climate zones and biomes, including comparing a contrasting region with the UK
Tropical rainforests are consistently hot (about 25–30°C) and receive over 2000 mm of rain per year, with little seasonal variation, producing ideal year-round growing conditions
learnerActions: Read or build a compare of three places — tropical rainforest, the UK (or your local area), and a hot desert — showing temperature and rainfall for each.

Record the numeric anchors: rainforest ~25–30°C and >2000 mm rain/year; note the UK as cooler, with less rain in most places (about 600–1200 mm/year in many areas, though some western hills get more) and clear seasons; note the desert as hot but very dry (often under 250 mm/year).
For each place, note how much life it supports and link it back to its temperature and rainfall.
Answer: which single factor most separates the rainforest from the desert? (water); and what are the main differences from the UK? (constant heat, much more rain, and no cold season).
Write one or two sentences explaining why the rainforest's figures produce fast year-round growth.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Hot and wet' becomes quantified and comparative: learners can say roughly how much hotter and wetter a rainforest is than their own climate and than a desert, and why those numbers matter.

activities.title: Weather today vs climate over years
feedback: If a learner expects a cold rainforest winter: contrast with the UK's seasons and restate that tropical climate stays hot and wet year-round.
If a learner uses 'it rained today' to describe climate: ask what the usual pattern is across whole years.
Confirm success when the learner keeps weather and climate distinct and links 'no off-season' to continuous growth.
activities.rationale: Distinguishing weather from climate is a common stumbling block at this age and underpins the 'all year' idea — the little-seasonal-variation, year-round growing conditions described in the source — that explains continuous growth and biodiversity.
sourceClaims: Tropical rainforests are consistently hot (about 25–30°C) and receive over 2000 mm of rain per year, with little seasonal variation, producing ideal year-round growing conditions
learnerActions: Compare a 'today's weather' statement (e.g. 'it is raining right now') with a 'climate' statement (e.g. 'it is hot and wet most of the year, every year').
Sort several example statements into 'weather (today)' or 'climate (usual long-term pattern)'.
Explain why a rainforest can have a rainy day and a drier day but still be described as hot and wet all year.
State that the rainforest climate has little seasonal change — unlike the UK's distinct seasons — so there is no cold season, and usually no long dry season, to stop plant growth.
activities.intendedInsight: Weather is what is happening now; climate is the usual pattern over many years. The rainforest's climate is consistently hot and wet with little seasonal variation, which is why plants can keep growing all year round.

activities.title: Explain the Sahara-vs-rainforest puzzle
feedback: If the learner says 'no real difference — both are just hot': this is the target misconception; contrast rainfall totals and name desert vs rainforest outcomes.
If the learner attributes growth to heat only: add the missing factor — abundant water — and ask what grows in a hot but dry place.

Model answer to compare against: 'The difference is water. The rainforest is hot AND very wet — over 2000 mm of rain a year and warm (25–30°C) all year — while the desert is hot but dry. The combination of constant heat and heavy rain lets plants grow fast all year and supports so much life; heat alone, as in a desert, is not enough.'
activities.rationale: A two-tier prompt (state the difference, then explain why) is intended to discriminate a child who thinks 'hot explains everything' from one who identifies rainfall and reasons about the combination; the reason-tier aims to elicit combination reasoning rather than fact recall. This diagnostic structure is an agent pedagogy proposal, not an efficacy claim backed by the cited sources.
learnerActions: Consider: the Sahara desert is hot; a rainforest is also hot — yet one has very little visible life and the other bursts with plants and animals.
State the difference in their climate (the desert is hot but dry; the rainforest is hot AND very wet).
Then explain WHY that difference matters so much (constant heat plus abundant water lets plants grow fast all year, supporting huge biodiversity; heat alone without water gives a desert).
Answer follow-up prompts: roughly how much more rain does a rainforest get than where you live? Does a rainforest have a cold winter? What would a hot place with almost no rain become?
activities.intendedInsight: The learner can independently articulate that rainfall is the key difference and that it is the heat-and-water combination that produces rapid growth and biodiversity.

constraints: Teach the two variables together with their consequence: hot AND wet → ideal year-round growth; do not let learners settle for 'it's hot'.
Always contrast with a hot DESERT to prove the combination (not heat alone) matters, and with the child's own/UK climate using real numbers.
Use the numeric anchors 25–30°C and >2000 mm/year so 'hot and wet' is quantified, not vague.
Explicitly distinguish weather (today) from climate (the usual multi-year pattern) and note the rainforest's little seasonal change.

A fixed comparison image or chart can teach the facts and comparison but does not let learners manipulate the variables; use it as a complement to, not a replacement for, variable-exploration when the goal is the combination insight.

Multiple-choice and matching formats, and estimate-on-a-scale checks, are useful for confirming recall and during hands-on exploration, but recognition-only responses do not elicit the learner's own explanation of WHY the combination matters — include a construct/explain activity for that objective.

The on-screen dials, growth meter, preset pins and greening/withering plot are optional illustrative mechanisms; an equivalent paper, card, or teacher-led version of 'change one variable at a time' meets the same objective.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Both source claims are marked verified:false in the row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy entry asserted that 'a static statement can't deliver' the combination insight and that '3D adds nothing over sliders and charts'. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established efficacy claims; they have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements. A fixed image can still teach the facts even if it cannot be manipulated.

Numeric anchors (25–30°C, >2000 mm/year) and the UK/desert contrast come from the sources and pedagogy fields; treat them as typical/approximate values, not precise constants for every rainforest. 'Little seasonal variation' is a source simplification; some rainforests show rainfall seasonality.
The 'cold hillside' / cool-and-wet preset is a plausible pedagogical contrast but is an illustrative scenario, not a claim about a specific named biome's exact figures.
The two-tier diagnostic rationale in the Sahara-vs-rainforest activity describes a pedagogical method; neither cited claim directly supports that method, so its sourceClaims list was set to [].

Independent re-audit: efficacy-flavoured wording in activity 2's rationale ('engages the learner beyond recognition') was softened to the observable affordance (production rather than recognition). The climate-facts claim retained on activities 1 and 3 supports the content/insight those activities teach, not the proposed interactive or sorting method, whose effectiveness remains untested.

probeDeeper: Roughly how much rain does a rainforest get compared with where you live?
Does a rainforest have a cold winter? What is its weather like across the year?
Why does the combination of heat and water grow plants faster than heat on its own?
What if a hot place got almost no rain — what kind of place would it become?
assess.correctAnswer: The difference is water. The rainforest is hot AND very wet — over 2000 mm of rain a year and warm (25–30°C) all year — while the desert is hot but dry. It's the COMBINATION of constant heat and constant heavy rain that lets plants grow fast all year and supports so much life. Heat alone (as in a desert) isn't enough; without the water you get a desert, not a rainforest.

errorPatterns.pattern: hot is what matters; a hot place is a hot place — doesn't see rainfall as the key difference
errorPatterns.nextMove: contrast rainfall totals; heat + heavy rain = rainforest, heat + little rain = desert
errorPatterns.distractor: There's no real difference — they're both just hot places
errorPatterns.revealedBy: can't say why a hot desert and a hot rainforest differ

errorPatterns.pattern: rainforests have seasons like the UK (hot summer, cold winter) — misses that it's hot and wet ALL year
errorPatterns.nextMove: tropical climate is consistently hot and wet year-round, unlike the UK's seasons
errorPatterns.revealedBy: describes a cold season in the rainforest

errorPatterns.pattern: heat alone makes things grow — 'it grows because it's warm'
errorPatterns.nextMove: it's heat AND abundant water together that drive the rapid growth
errorPatterns.revealedBy: attributes lush growth to heat only, omitting water

responseLevels.gap: Thinks 'hot' explains everything; can't distinguish rainforest from desert climate.
responseLevels.full: Identifies rainfall as the key difference, describes a consistently hot AND wet year-round climate (~25–30°C, >2000 mm), and explains the combination drives rapid growth and biodiversity, contrasting a hot dry desert.
responseLevels.partial: Knows rainforests are hot and wet but treats heat and rain separately, or expects UK-style seasons.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: The Sahara desert is hot. A rainforest is also hot. Both are hot places — so why does one become a lifeless-looking desert and the other burst with plants and animals? Tell me the difference in their climate, and then tell me WHY that difference matters so much.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding 'hot is the whole story' can't explain why deserts and rainforests differ; the concept child identifies rainfall as the difference and stresses the heat-AND-water combination. The reason-tier forces the combination reasoning.
